what: Casella Waste Systems collects and disposes of rubbish in the northeastern United States. It runs collection routes, transfer stations, recycling plants and, most importantly, landfills, in a region where new landfill capacity is almost impossible to permit.
customers: Households and businesses on municipal and commercial collection contracts, plus other haulers who must pay to dispose of waste at Casella’s landfills and transfer stations.
money: Residential and commercial rubbish collection under municipal and private contracts.
Landfill tipping fees, including from third-party haulers, and transfer station throughput.
Processing and selling recovered materials, and national accounts brokerage.
moat: Landfills in the Northeast are the asset. Permitting a new one in New England is effectively impossible, existing capacity is filling, and waste still has to go somewhere, so whoever owns the hole in the ground sets the price for the whole region. Owning both the collection routes and the disposal site means Casella captures the margin twice and can squeeze independent haulers who depend on its landfills.
risks: The trailing period shows a small net loss of about $11.3M, and the shares trade at about 19.98 times EV/EBITDA and 78 times free cash flow.
Growth has come heavily from acquiring small haulers, which adds goodwill and integration work and means reported results flatter the underlying business.
Debt of $1.2B against $123.8M of cash has risen with that acquisition programme.
Recycled commodity prices move independently of the rest of the business and can swing the resource solutions segment from profit to loss.
Ten analysts average a $107.50 target, only about 9% above the current price, so little upside is priced in even by the optimists.
opportunities: Revenue has doubled, from $889.2M in 2021 to $1.8B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $2.0B.
Waste volumes are the most recession-resistant revenue in the industrial economy: households and shops produce rubbish regardless of the cycle.
Landfill scarcity in the Northeast gives Casella genuine pricing power, and it has raised prices above inflation for years.
The regional hauling market is still fragmented, so there is a long list of small operators to acquire and fold into existing routes.
watch: Pricing above inflation and landfill capacity remaining. Volume growth can be bought; price increases that stick are what prove the regional position is as strong as the valuation assumes.
view: Waste is one of the few genuinely good businesses hiding in plain sight, and the reason is physical rather than financial: rubbish has to go somewhere, and in the northeastern United States there is almost nowhere new to put it. Casella owns the holes in the ground across New England and upstate New York, collects the waste that goes into them, and charges competitors for the privilege of using them. That is as close to a regulated monopoly as an unregulated company gets, and it is why this has compounded for two decades.

What I would push back on is the price. At roughly 20 times EV/EBITDA and 78 times free cash flow, with a small trailing net loss, the market is paying a premium even against Waste Management and Republic Services, which are larger, more diversified and more profitable. The justification offered is the pricing power from landfill scarcity plus a long runway of small haulers to acquire. Both are real. But the valuation leaves no room for the acquisition machine to stumble, and acquisition-led growth is precisely the kind that looks better in reported revenue than in per-share value. Revenue doubling from $889 million to $2.0 billion is impressive; how much of it was bought, and at what multiple, is the question the headline does not answer.

The quality of the earnings deserves scrutiny too. Free cash flow of $81 million against $2.0 billion of revenue is thin for a waste company, because landfill development, cell construction and fleet replacement absorb cash continuously, and acquisitions absorb more. The industry convention of judging these businesses on EBITDA exists partly because it is flattering: it sits above the very real capital spending that owning landfills and trucks requires. I would rather underwrite this on cash flow per share after all of that, and on that basis the multiple is demanding.

None of which makes it a bad holding. It makes it a good business at a full price, which is a different problem from a cheap stock with a flaw. The ten analysts averaging $107.50, barely 9% above the market, are telling you roughly the same thing in their own language: nobody thinks this is mispriced, everybody thinks it is well run. The case for owning it is that pricing power in a capacity-constrained region compounds quietly for a very long time and you will never buy it cheaply. The case for waiting is that at this multiple a single bad recycling year or an indigestible acquisition costs you several years of that compounding. Watch price increases net of volume, and watch what is paid for each tuck-in.
bull: Landfill scarcity keeps supporting above-inflation price increases while tuck-in acquisitions densify existing routes, and a small-cap compounder keeps compounding.
bear: Acquisition multiples rise, recycling prices turn, and 20 times EBITDA for a business with thin free cash flow leaves nothing for a single bad year.
